newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica's labour court rules against Cosatu strike.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica's labour court rules against Cosatu strike.

text.p: South Africa's Labour Appeal Court on Friday ruled against the Congress of South African Trade Union's planned half-day strike action on May 12.
The court said in its judgment that the planned protest action did not comply with section 77(1)(c) of the Labour Relations Act (LRA).

"...the matter giving rise to the intended protest action had not been considered by the National Economic Development and Labour Council and consequently...any person who takes part in the protest action on May 12 by a witdrawal of labour does not enjoy the protections conferred by section 67 of the Act," the judgment said.
It advised the Congress of South African Trade Union (Cosatu) to inform affiliates that the protest action was in breach of section 77 of the Act.
The court ordered Cosatu to pay costs of the application.
Cosatu has called the protest action over the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill which has threatened to become a flashpoint between trade unions and business.
The bill was approved by cabinet in April and is now before the tri-partite National Economic Development and Labour Council (Nedlac) for discussion.
Cosatu wants to ensure its demands relating specifically to a 40-hour working week and six months paid maternity leave are not watered down when the bill is eventually tabled in parliament.
In an initial reaction, Business South Africa (BSA) negotiator Adrian du Plessis welcomed the judgment and said employers were open to further talks on the employment bill.
"We welcome the judgment and are ready to resume negotiations in Nedlac tomorrow (Saturday) on the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill," du Plessis said.
Cosatu will respond later on Friday to the court's decision.
But the federation reiterated this week that it would go ahead with the planned protest despite the interdict served by BSA this week aimed at preventing the half-day strike.
In line with the Green Paper released in February last year, the employment bill retains proposals to reduce weekly working hours to 45 from 46 hours, including mine, farm and shift workers.
It proposes a large reduction in working hours for security workers from 60 hours a week to 45 hours.

The bill, which for the first time also includes public service employees, also proposes an increase in overtime pay from time-and-a-third to time-and-a-half -- a proposal that employers are strongly opposed to.
